q: What were the open rooms on either side of the atrium called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Alae were open rooms located on each side of the atrium.

q: By what two other names is the Basilica of Constantine, in the Forum Romanum, known?
o: The Basilica of Maxentius, or Basilica Nova
The Basilica Ulpia, or Basilica of Trajan
The Basilica Argentaria, or Basilica of Domitian
The Basilica Aemilia, or Basilica of Julia
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Basilicas
n: The Basilica of Constantine in the Forum Romanum is also known as the Basilica of Maxentius or Basilica Nova.

q: What was the kitchen of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Cullina was the kitchen of the domus.

q: What did the word "Thermae" originally, properly mean?
o: Warm springs, or baths of warm water
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: "Thermae" properly meant warm springs or baths of warm water.

q: What was the small garden of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Peristylium was the small garden of a domus.

q: Which Roman bath complex was the largest and grandest, accommodating about 3,000 bathers?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Thermae of Diocletian, commissioned by Maximian, were the largest and grandest Roman baths, accommodating about 3,000 bathers.

q: What was a large communal dining room or lounge, distinct from the triclinium, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Exedra was a large communal dining room or lounge.

q: Whose mural designs decorated the Baths of Titus?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Baths of Titus were noted for mural designs by Famullus, or Fabullus.

q: What was the small initial opening or entrance of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Ostium was the small opening that served as the initial entrance of a domus.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths was the hot room, or hot water bath?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Calidarium was the hot room, or hot water bath.

q: What did the first Pompeian wall-painting style imitate?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The first Pompeian painting style imitated ashlar masonry.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths provided a moist steam bath?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Sudatorium provided a moist steam bath.

q: What was the focus of the third Pompeian wall-painting style?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The third Pompeian painting style focused on mystical creatures.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths served as the dressing room?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Apodyteria was the dressing room of the large Imperial baths.

q: What features generally characterized a Roman villa?
o: Surrounding terraces and gardens, colonnades, palaestrae, and thermae
A fortified perimeter wall with watchtowers
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Villa
n: A Roman villa was a luxurious country house with surrounding terraces and gardens, colonnades, palaestrae (exercise grounds), and thermae.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths held oils and perfumes?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Thermae
n: The Unctuaria was the room for oils and perfumes.

q: Who typically occupied the Villa Rustica portion of a Roman country estate?
o: The servants generally in charge of the estate
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Roman Houses — Villa and Insula
n: The Villa Rustica, or country house, was permanently occupied by the servants generally in charge of the estate.

q: Where is Hadrian's Villa Summer Bath located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Balneum
n: Hadrian's Villa Summer Bath is located at Tivoli, Italy.

q: Who typically lived in Roman insulae?
o: Most of the urban citizen population, including ordinary people of lower- or middle-class status (the plebs)
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Roman Houses — Villa and Insula
n: Insulae housed most of the urban citizen population of ancient Rome, including ordinary people of lower- or middle-class status, the plebs.

q: To which god was the Serapeum at Hadrian's Villa dedicated?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Balneum
n: The Serapeum at Hadrian's Villa was dedicated to the god Serapis; Canopus was the Egyptian city where a temple to Serapis stood.

q: What is the Pont du Gard, and what larger structure is it part of?
o: A bridge that forms part of an aqueduct
A section of city defensive wall
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Aqueducts
n: The Pont du Gard (Gard Bridge) is part of the aqueduct built by the Romans to carry water to Nimes.

q: What distinguishes a "balneum" from the great public thermae?
o: A balneum had no heated rooms at all
A balneum was reserved for gladiators only
A balneum was always built underground
A balneum was a private bath within Roman palaces and houses
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Balneum
n: A balneum was a private bath found in Roman palaces and houses, typically containing its own tepidarium, calidarium, and frigidarium.

q: What did this aqueduct carry, and between which two points?
o: Wine, from vineyards near Nimes to Uzes
Stone, from a quarry at Uzes to Nimes
Grain, from Uzes to the port at Nimes
Water, from a spring at Uzes to the Roman colony of Nemausus (Nimes)
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Aqueducts
n: The aqueduct carried water from a spring at Uzes to the Roman colony of Nemausus, present-day Nimes.

q: What was the seating capacity of the Theater of Marcellus?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: The Theater of Marcellus held between 15,000 and 20,500 spectators.

q: Which was the earliest known bridge of ancient Rome, and what was it made of?
o: The Pons Mulvius, made of stone
The Pons Sublicius, made entirely of wood
The Pont du Gard, made of marble
The Bridge of Augustus, made of brick
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: The Pons Sublicius was the earliest known bridge of ancient Rome, made entirely of wood.

q: What order of columns appeared on the lower tier of the Theater of Marcellus, and what order on the second tier?
o: Corinthian on the lower tier, Doric on the second
Doric on the lower tier, Ionic on the second
Ionic on the lower tier, Doric on the second
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: The lower tier of the Theater of Marcellus had Doric columns, the second tier Ionic, with the top attic probably carrying Corinthian pilasters.

q: Which famous battle took place at the Pons Mulvius?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: The Pons Mulvius was the site of the famous Battle of Milvian Bridge.

q: Unlike Greek theaters cut into natural hillsides, how were Roman theaters typically constructed?
o: Built with wooden scaffolding left permanently in place
Suspended on iron cables between towers
Built up from level ground using concrete vaulting to support tiers of seats
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: Roman theaters were open-air structures built from level ground, using concrete vaulting to support their tiers of seats, unlike Greek theaters built into hillsides.

q: In the 2000s, what modern romantic tradition became associated with the Pons Mulvius?
o: Couples attaching love padlocks to a lamppost on the bridge
Couples lighting lanterns and releasing them from the bridge
Couples exchanging vows in a chapel beside the bridge
Couples tossing coins into the river below
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: Since the 2000s, the Pons Mulvius has attracted couples who attach love padlocks to a lamppost on the bridge as a token of love.

q: What are the approximate dimensions of the elliptical Colosseum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Colosseum's elliptical footprint measures about 188 by 156 meters.

q: What general design principle guided the construction of Roman bridges?
o: Lightweight, temporary construction meant to be rebuilt yearly
Elaborate decoration prioritized over structural strength
Construction entirely without the use of arches
Simple, solid, and practical construction designed to resist the rush of water
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: Roman bridges were built with simple, solid, and practical construction, designed to resist the rush of water.

q: How many larger-than-life statues graced the arches of the Colosseum's upper floors?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The marble-clad Colosseum displayed 160 larger-than-life statues on its upper-floor arches.

q: Who added the second fountain in St. Peter's Square, about half a century after Maderno's?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: Gian Lorenzo Bernini added a second fountain to St. Peter's Square in 1677, half a century after Maderno's original.

q: Through how many entrances could spectators enter the Colosseum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: Spectators entered the Colosseum through no less than 80 entrances.

q: What figure does the Triton Fountain at Piazza Barberini represent?
o: Neptune riding a chariot of seahorses
A wingless victory descending from the sky
Triton, half-man and half-fish, blowing his horn to calm the waters
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Triton Fountain, a masterpiece of Baroque sculpture, represents Triton, half-man and half-fish, blowing his horn to calm the waters.

q: Which groups of spectators sat in the Colosseum's upper story?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Colosseum's upper story provided seating for the lower classes and for women, while the lowest story was preserved for prominent citizens.

q: Who designed the Triton Fountain at Piazza Barberini?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Triton Fountain was designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini.

q: How could animals confined beneath the Colosseum be brought up into the arena?
o: They were led up long ramps by handlers
Their cages could be hoisted up
They were lowered in from the upper stands
They were released through side gates at ground level
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The underground cages holding wild animals could be hoisted up, enabling the animals to appear in the middle of the arena.

q: Who designed the two fountains at either end of Piazza Navona?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: Giacomo della Porta designed the fountains at either end of Piazza Navona, including the Neptune Fountain to the north.

q: What kinds of events took place at the Circus Maximus?
o: Various games, horse races, and chariot races
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Circus Maximus provided various games as well as horse and chariot races.

q: What does La Fontana del Moro, at the south end of Piazza Navona, depict?
o: A wingless victory descending to earth
Four rivers of the four continents
A figure of either an African (Moor) or Neptune, wrestling with a dolphin
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: La Fontana del Moro shows a figure, either an African (a Moor) or Neptune, wrestling with a dolphin.

q: What general shape describes the auditorium of a Roman amphitheater?
o: Strictly square with seating on only two sides
A narrow rectangle with seating at one end
Circular, semi-circular, or elliptical, with rising tiers of seats around a central arena
A star-shaped plan with seating on each point
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: A Roman amphitheater's auditorium was circular, semi-circular, or elliptical, with a central arena surrounded by rising tiers of seats.

q: Which four rivers are represented by statues at the Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi?
o: The Danube, the Rhine, the Po, and the Tiber
The Nile, the Danube, the Plate (Río de la Plata), and the Ganges
The Ganges, the Yangtze, the Amazon, and the Congo
The Nile, the Tiber, the Seine, and the Thames
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi features statues representing rivers from the four continents: the Nile, the Danube, the Plate, and the Ganges.

q: What event does the Arch of Titus, in Rome, commemorate?
o: The recovery of the Aquila standards
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Triumphal Arches
n: The Arch of Titus commemorates the capture of Jerusalem.

q: Roughly how tall is the Egyptian obelisk at the center of Piazza Navona?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The obelisk at the center of Piazza Navona stands about 54 feet, or 16 meters, tall.

q: What event does the Arch of Constantine commemorate?
o: The recovery of the Aquila standards
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Triumphal Arches
n: The Arch of Constantine commemorates his triumph over Maxentius.

q: Who designed the Trevi Fountain?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Trevi Fountain was the work of the architect Nicola Salvi, carried forward through the successive patronage of several popes.

q: Where is the Porta Nigra, one of the best-preserved city gateways, located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Town Gateways
n: The Porta Nigra, part of the city walls and one of the best-preserved gateways of its kind, is located at Treves.

q: In what does the Oceanus figure at the Trevi Fountain ride?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: Oceanus rides in an oyster-shell chariot at the center of the Trevi Fountain, surrounded by Tritons and Sea Nymphs.

q: How was the court behind the Porta Nigra's double archway defended against besiegers?
o: It was sealed permanently with masonry
It was flooded with water from a nearby aqueduct
It was an unroofed court defended by portcullises
It was ringed with iron spikes
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: The Porta Nigra's double archway led to an unroofed court that could be defended against besiegers by portcullises.

q: For centuries, what role did the Forum Romanum play in Roman public life?
o: It served exclusively as a marketplace for grain
It hosted triumphal processions, elections, public speeches, criminal trials, gladiatorial matches, and commercial affairs
It was reserved solely for religious sacrifices
It functioned only as a military parade ground
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Forum
n: The Forum Romanum was used for triumphal processions, elections, public speeches, criminal trials, gladiatorial matches, and as the hub of commercial affairs.

q: How many archways does the Port S. Andre gateway at Autun have, and what were they intended for?
o: Four — two for carriages and two for foot-passengers
Six — three for carriages and three for foot-passengers
One large archway shared by all traffic
Two — one for carriages and one for foot-passengers
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: Port S. Andre is an unusual gateway with four archways: two for carriages and two for foot-passengers.

q: To which god is the Temple of Fortuna Virilis, in the Forum Boarium, dedicated?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Fortuna Virilis (Temio di Portuno) is the main temple dedicated to the god Portunus, built in the Ionic order with a pronaos portico.

q: How does a second gateway at Autun differ in design from Port S. Andre?
o: It has twice as many archways
Its arcaded gallery uses Corinthian, rather than Ionic, pilasters
It uses Doric columns instead of pilasters
It has no arcaded gallery at all
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: Another gateway at Autun is similar in design to Port S. Andre, except that the pilasters of its arcaded gallery are Corinthian instead of Ionic.

q: Where does the Temple of Mars Ultor stand, and what role did it play in Roman military life?
o: The Forum Boarium; it was a marketplace shrine
The Forum of Augustus, Rome; it was the focal point of Roman military strategy
Ostia; it served as a naval command post
The Capitoline Hill; it housed the state treasury
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Mars Ultor, in the Corinthian order, stood in the Forum of Augustus and was the focal point of Roman military strategy.

q: What order of column is Trajan's Column, and what material is it made of?
o: Composite, made of brick and stucco
Roman Doric, made entirely of marble
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Pillars of Victory or Monumental Columns
n: Trajan's Column is a Roman Doric column made entirely of marble.

q: What order and plan describe the Temple of Vespasian?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Vespasian used the Corinthian order in a hexastyle, prostyle plan.

q: What internal feature allows one to ascend Trajan's Column?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Pillars of Victory or Monumental Columns
n: Trajan's Column contains a spiral staircase within its shaft.

q: Who is credited as architect of the Temple of Saturn (Templum Saturni) in the Forum Romanum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Saturn in the Forum Romanum is credited to Tarquinis Superbus.

q: Which Roman palace, at Spalato, was often nicknamed "a city in a house"?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: The Palace of Diocletian at Spalato, the largest Roman palace, was often called "a city in a house."

q: Roughly how large was Hadrian's Temple of Venus in Rome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Venus measured an impressive 100 by 145 meters, among the largest religious structures of ancient Rome.

q: How many rooms did the Golden House of Nero (Domus Aurea) contain?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: Nero's Golden House contained 300 rooms.

q: Where is the Maison-Carrée located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Maison-Carrée ("Square House") stands at Nimes, France.

q: What materials decorated the stuccoed ceilings of the Golden House of Nero?
o: Semi-precious stones, ivory, and gold leaf
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: The Golden House of Nero featured stuccoed ceilings set with semi-precious stones and layers of ivory and gold leaf.

q: What order and plan describe the Maison-Carrée?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Maison-Carrée is an elevated, rectangular, hexastyle, pseudo-peripteral temple of the Corinthian order, about 25 by 12 meters.

q: What social classes typically occupied a Roman domus?
o: The upper classes and some wealthy freedmen
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The domus was the type of house occupied by the upper classes and some wealthy freedmen during the Republican and Imperial eras.

q: On what were Roman rectangular temples typically raised, and toward which direction were they generally oriented?
o: Ground level, oriented toward the east
A podium, oriented toward the south
An artificial mound, with no fixed orientation
A stepped crepidoma, oriented toward the north
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: Roman rectangular temples were raised on a podium and generally oriented toward the south, though orientation could vary depending on the temple's relationship to nearby civic buildings.

q: What was the square opening in the roof, through which rainwater entered the atrium, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Compluvium was the square roof opening through which rainwater drained inward from the slanted tiled roof.

q: Which circular Roman temple was considered the most sacred shrine and source of Roman life and power?
o: The Temple of Venus at Baalbek
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: The Temple of Vesta in Rome was regarded as the most sacred shrine and source of Roman life and power.

q: What was the main entrance hall of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Vestibulum was the main entrance hall of a domus.

q: What is the Pantheon in Rome especially noted for?
o: Being the largest circular temple ever built
Housing the tomb of Julius Caesar
Being built entirely of imported Egyptian granite
Being the most famous and best-preserved of all ancient buildings in Rome
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: The Pantheon is the most famous and best-preserved of all ancient buildings in Rome.

q: What were the shops facing the street, on the outside of a domus, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Tabernae were shops located on the outside of the domus, facing the street.

q: Roman circular and polygonal temples derived their form from the temples of which earlier civilizations?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: Roman circular and polygonal temples were derived from the temples of the Greeks and the Etruscans.

q: What was the dining room furnished with reclining couches called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Triclinium was the dining room, furnished with recliners.

q: Who designed Trajan's Basilica in Rome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Basilicas
n: Trajan's Basilica in Rome was designed by Apollodorus of Damascus.

q: What was a bedroom in a Roman domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Cubiculum was the bedroom of a Roman domus.

q: What was the general function of a Roman basilica?
o: A hall of justice or an assembly hall
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Basilicas
n: Roman basilicas generally served as halls of justice or assembly halls, as with Trajan's Basilica and the Basilica of Constantine.

q: What was the servants' entrance of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Posticum served as the servants' entrance to the domus.

q: Which Roman bath complex was the second largest, accommodating about 1,600 bathers?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Baths of Caracalla (Terme di Caracalla), built under Septimius Severus, were the second largest thermae, holding about 1,600 bathers.

q: What was the fish pond of a domus called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Piscina was the fish pond of a domus.

q: Who commissioned the Thermae of Diocletian?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Thermae of Diocletian were commissioned by Maximian.

q: What was the small household shrine of a domus, dedicated to the household gods, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Lararium was a small shrine to the household gods.

q: In the large Imperial baths, which room was the warm room?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Tepidarium was the warm room of the large Imperial baths.

q: Wall paintings inside a Pompeian domus are generally grouped into how many recognized styles?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: Pompeian domus interiors are grouped into four recognized painting styles.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths served as the cooling room?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Thermae
n: The Frigidarium was the cooling room of the large Imperial baths.

q: What did the second Pompeian wall-painting style represent?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The second Pompeian painting style represented public architecture.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths was the dry sweating room, similar to a sauna?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Thermae
n: The Laconium was the dry sweating room, akin to a modern sauna.

q: What did the fourth Pompeian wall-painting style do?
o: Introduced portraiture of the homeowner's family
Returned entirely to plain, undecorated walls
Combined the architecture of the second style with the mythical creatures of the third
Combined ashlar masonry with geometric mosaics
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The fourth Pompeian painting style combined the architecture of the second style and the mythical creatures of the third style.

q: Which area of the large Imperial baths was used for physical exercise?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Thermae
n: The Palaestra was the area used for physical exercise.

q: What distinguished a Villa Urbana from a Villa Rustica?
o: The Villa Urbana was always larger than the Villa Rustica
The Villa Urbana was a country seat for a short stay near a city, while the Villa Rustica was a permanently occupied farm-house estate
There was no real difference between the two
The Villa Rustica was reserved for the emperor's family
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Roman Houses — Villa and Insula
n: The Villa Urbana was a country seat that could easily be reached from Rome or another city for a night or two, while the Villa Rustica was the farm-house estate permanently occupied by the servants generally in charge of it.

q: Which room of the large Imperial baths functioned as a game room?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Thermae
n: The Spaeresterium served as the game room of the large Imperial baths.

q: What was an insula in ancient Rome?
o: An artificial island in the Tiber
A many-storeyed apartment building, or tenement
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Roman Houses — Villa and Insula
n: The insula was a many-storeyed tenement, a kind of apartment building.

q: What are the pool and artificial grotto at Hadrian's Villa named?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Balneum
n: The pool and artificial grotto at Hadrian's Villa were named Canopus and Serapeum, respectively.

q: By what other name was the insula sometimes known?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Roman Houses — Villa and Insula
n: The insula was also called "Workmen's Dwelling."

q: What stylistic influence is visible in the Corinthian columns and Greek statue copies surrounding the pool at Hadrian's Villa?
o: Etruscan influence, typical of the early Republic
Greek influence, typical of Roman architecture of the High and Late Empire
Persian influence, typical of the Achaemenid court
Egyptian influence, typical of the Old Kingdom
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Balneum
n: The architecture surrounding Hadrian's Villa pool is Greek-influenced, typical of Roman architecture of the High and Late Empire, seen in its Corinthian columns and copies of famous Greek statues.

q: Roughly how long is the aqueduct that the Pont du Gard belongs to?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Aqueducts
n: The aqueduct associated with the Pont du Gard runs about 50 km, or 31 miles.

q: Which was the largest and most important theatre in Rome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: The Theater of Marcellus was the largest and most important theatre in Rome.

q: Apart from underground sections, how were Roman aqueduct channels often built when crossing valleys or low ground?
o: Routed around obstacles at ground level
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Aqueducts
n: Roman aqueduct channels were often underground, but were treated architecturally on high arches when crossing valleys or low ground, as at the Pont du Gard.

q: How many arches composed each tier of the Theater of Marcellus's semicircular travertine facade?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: Each of the two original tiers of the Theater of Marcellus's facade was composed of 41 arches.

q: Who is credited with building the Pons Sublicius?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: The Pons Sublicius is credited to Ancus Marcius.

q: Which Roman theater is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and considered the best-preserved theatre in all of Europe?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: Theater Orange is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is designated the best preserved theatre in the whole of Europe.

q: Who is credited with the Pons Mulvius?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: The Pons Mulvius is credited to Gaius Claudius Nero.

q: What shape were Roman theaters, such as the Theater of Marcellus, generally restricted to?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Theaters / Odeion
n: Roman theaters were richly decorated open-air structures restricted to a semi-circular plan.

q: In which city is the Bridge of Augustus located?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Bridges or Pons
n: The Bridge of Augustus stands at Rimini.

q: To roughly what height does the Colosseum rise?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Colosseum reaches a height of more than 48 meters, or about 159 feet.

q: Who designed the earlier (1614) fountain in St. Peter's Square?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: Carlo Maderno designed the 1614 fountain in St. Peter's Square, made to complement his lavish Baroque facade for the Basilica.

q: What was the Colosseum's approximate spectator capacity?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Colosseum could accommodate roughly 55,000 spectators.

q: What did Maderno's 1614 fountain in St. Peter's Square reuse from an even earlier fountain on the same site, dating to 1490?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: Maderno's fountain was built on the site of an earlier fountain from 1490 and reused the same lower basin.

q: Who commenced construction of the Colosseum, and who completed it?
o: Commenced by Hadrian, completed by Trajan
Commenced by Domitian, completed by Vespasian
Commenced by Titus, completed by Nero
Commenced by Vespasian, completed by Domitian
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: Construction of the Colosseum was commenced by Vespasian and completed by Domitian.

q: Whose literary work inspired the design of the Triton Fountain?
o: Livy, in his History of Rome
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Triton Fountain follows a text by the Roman poet Ovid in the Metamorphoses.

q: What lay beneath the arena floor of the Colosseum?
o: Rooms with mechanical devices and cages for wild animals
Storage for grain and olive oil
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: Below the arena floor, the Colosseum housed rooms with mechanical devices and cages holding wild animals.

q: On the site of which earlier structure were the fountains of Piazza Navona built?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Piazza Navona fountains form a "grand theater of water" built on the site of the Stadium of Domitian.

q: What was the approximate spectator capacity of the Circus Maximus?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: The Circus Maximus was a massive arena accommodating some 250,000 spectators.

q: What does the Neptune Fountain (1572), at the north end of Piazza Navona, depict?
o: Four river gods representing the continents
Triton alone, blowing a conch shell
The god of the sea sparring, surrounded by an octopus, tritons, sea horses, and mermaids
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Neptune Fountain shows the god of the sea sparring, surrounded by an octopus, tritons, sea horses, and mermaids.

q: What shape did a Roman circus, as distinct from an amphitheater, generally take, and what was it used for?
o: A triangular shape used for naval demonstrations
A square used for military drills
A roofless, oblong enclosure for chariot or horse racing and gladiator shows
A perfect circle used solely for religious processions
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Amphitheaters / Colosseum
n: A circus was a roofless enclosure, usually oblong in shape, used for chariot or horse racing and gladiator shows.

q: Who designed the central Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi (Fountain of the Four Rivers) at Piazza Navona?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The highly theatrical Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi at the center of Piazza Navona (1648-51) was designed by Bernini.

q: What event does the Arch of Tiberius at Orange, France commemorate?
o: The recovery of the eagle standards (Aquila) lost to Germanic tribes by Varus in AD 9
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Triumphal Arches
n: The Arch of Tiberius at Orange commemorates the recovery of the eagle standards that had been lost to Germanic tribes by Varus in AD 9.

q: What tops the Egyptian obelisk at the center of Piazza Navona, and whose emblem does it carry?
o: A cross bearing the emblem of the Pamphili family, representing Pope Innocent X
A bronze statue of Bernini himself
A gilded eagle representing the Roman Senate
A weathervane in the shape of a dolphin
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The obelisk over the Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi is crowned with a cross bearing the emblem of the Pamphili family, representing Pope Innocent X.

q: What event does the Arch of Septimius Severus commemorate?
o: The recovery of the Aquila standards
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Triumphal Arches
n: The Arch of Septimius Severus commemorates victories against the Parthians.

q: At the terminus of which reconstructed aqueduct was the Trevi Fountain built, beginning in 1730?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The Trevi Fountain, the largest and most spectacular of Rome's fountains, was built beginning in 1730 at the terminus of the reconstructed Acqua Vergine aqueduct.

q: What was the general function of Roman triumphal arches?
o: To mark the boundary of the sacred pomerium
To house the remains of fallen soldiers
To serve as fortified checkpoints along the frontier
To commemorate imperial victories with reliefs, inscriptions, and statues
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 39 — Triumphal Arches
n: Triumphal arches functioned to commemorate imperial victories, decorated with reliefs, inscriptions, and statues.

q: Who is the central figure of the Trevi Fountain, personifying all the seas and oceans?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 41 — Fountains
n: The central figure of the Trevi Fountain is Oceanus, the personification of all the seas and oceans.

q: What are the approximate dimensions of the Porta Nigra at its highest and widest points?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: The Porta Nigra measures 115 feet wide and 95 feet high at its highest part.

q: Where in Rome was the Forum Romanum located?
o: In the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline Hills
Outside the city walls near the Colosseum
On the summit of the Capitoline Hill
Along the banks of the Tiber River
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Forum
n: The Forum Romanum sat in the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline Hills, and served for centuries as the center of Roman public life.

q: What classical order do the Porta Nigra's roughly executed, unfinished facade storeys use?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: The Porta Nigra's facade has storeys of roughly executed, unfinished Tuscan order.

q: Which Roman forum was the site of the city's first gladiatorial contest?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Forum
n: The Forum Boarium is recorded as the site of Rome's first gladiatorial contest.

q: What decorates the arcaded gallery above the Port S. Andre gateway at Autun?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: Port S. Andre is surmounted by an arcaded gallery decorated with Ionic pilasters, connecting ramparts on either side.

q: What porch arrangement and order define the Temple of Fortuna Virilis?
o: Ionic order with a pronaos portico
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Fortuna Virilis is built in the Ionic order and includes a pronaos portico.

q: Where did Romans sometimes place gateways along a bridge, as seen at the Roman bridge at Alcantara?
o: On temporary pontoons beside the bridge
Only at the midpoint of the riverbed
At the ends, or at the centre over the central pier
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Town Gateways and Archways
n: Gateways were sometimes added either at the ends of bridges or at the centre, as at the Roman bridge at Alcantara, which has a portal over the central pier.

q: How many Ionic columns does the Temple of Diana, on the Aventine Hill in Nimes, have?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Diana is recorded as having 127 Ionic columns.

q: What is the total height of Trajan's Column?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Pillars of Victory or Monumental Columns
n: Trajan's Column stands a total of 115 feet, 7 inches tall, with a shaft diameter of 12 inches.

q: On which hill stood the Temple of Jupiter, considered the most important temple in Ancient Rome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Jupiter, Ancient Rome's most important temple, was located on the Capitoline Hill.

q: What did Roman Rostral Columns commemorate, and where did their name originate?
o: Naval victories; named for the rostra, the rows of captured ships' prows used to decorate them
Imperial coronations; named for a ceremonial robe
Military conquests on land; named for the rostrum from which generals gave speeches
Religious festivals; named for a mythical sea creature
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Pillars of Victory or Monumental Columns
n: Rostral Columns were erected to celebrate naval victories, taking their name from the rostra — rows of captured ships' prows — used to ornament them.

q: Who designed the Temple of Venus in Rome, built at the end of the Forum Romanum near the Colosseum?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Venus, an impressive structure near the Colosseum, was designed by Emperor Hadrian in 135 AD.

q: Roughly how large was the Palace of Diocletian, and to what is it compared in size?
o: About 2 acres, the size of a city block
About 20 acres, the size of a small town
About 8 acres, almost the size of the Escorial in Spain
About 1 acre, the size of a single villa
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: The Palace of Diocletian covered a total of about 8 acres, almost the size of the Escorial in Spain.

q: How many cellae (shrines) did the Temple of Venus in Rome contain, and what did each hold?
o: Four, one for each cardinal direction
One, holding statues of both goddesses together
Three, arranged around a central altar
Two, each holding a statue of a goddess
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Temple of Venus contained two cellae, each holding a statue of a goddess, located on either side of the temple.

q: What unusual mechanical feature did a room in the Golden House of Nero have?
o: A hidden trapdoor to the sewers
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: The Golden House of Nero was noted for having a rotating ceiling in one of its rooms.

q: Who built the Maison-Carrée?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: The Maison-Carrée was built by Agrippa.

q: What was built on the site of the demolished Golden House of Nero?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Palaces
n: The Golden House of Nero was demolished, and the Roman Colosseum was built on its site.

q: What does "pseudo-peripteral," a plan common to many Roman rectangular temples, describe?
o: A circular temple with no colonnade at all
A temple with columns only on the front
Half-columns attached to the naos wall rather than a full freestanding colonnade
A temple with two complete rows of freestanding columns
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: Roman rectangular temples typically used a pseudo-peripteral plan: half-columns attached to the naos wall, raised on a podium, rather than a full ring of freestanding columns.

q: What was the large central hall of a domus, considered its most important room, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Atrium was the large central hall of a domus, and its most important part.

q: What generally governed the orientation of a Roman temple, beyond a simple compass direction?
o: Its relationship to nearby buildings, especially facing onto a forum or civic space
The position of the nearest aqueduct
Strict alignment with the rising sun each equinox
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Rectangular Temples
n: Roman temples were turned to all parts of the compass; their orientation was governed by their relationship to other buildings, often facing onto civic spaces such as the forum.

q: What was the shallow, sunken pool beneath the compluvium, which collected rainwater into an underground cistern, called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Impluvium was a shallow rectangular sunken pool in the atrium that drained rainwater into an underground cistern.

q: How many columns did the Temple of Venus at Baalbek have, likely once supporting a dome?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: The Temple of Venus at Baalbek has six columns that probably once supported a dome, and was carved with niches and sculptures throughout.

q: What was the narrow corridor from the main door to the atrium called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Fauces was the corridor connecting the main door to the atrium.

q: What did the Pantheon become, which helped preserve it through the centuries?
o: A Christian church, named Santa Maria Rotonda
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: The Pantheon was converted into a Christian church named Santa Maria Rotonda, which contributed to its remarkable preservation.

q: What was the living room, study, or office of the head of the household (dominus) called?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 40 — Roman Houses — Domus
n: The Tablinum served as a living room, study, or office for the dominus.

q: Roman circular temples became the architectural prototype for what later Christian building type?
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 38 — Circular and Polygonal Temples
n: Roman circular temples became the prototype for the Christian baptistery.
